opening: When a community loses the person who united it, what gives someone else the authority to lead?
setting: An imagined courtyard. An interpretive setting, not a reconstruction of a documented place.
shared: Sunni and Shi'a Muslims belong to Islam and share central beliefs and practices, including belief in one God, the Qur'an, and prayer. Their traditions developed over time.
invitation: What does this older history help you notice, and what would you still need to learn about this conflict?

moments.title: A question of succession
moments.label: Succession
moments.body: After Muhammad died in 632, Abu Bakr became the first caliph, the leader of the Muslim community. Supporters of Ali understood rightful leadership differently. The question of who should lead, and on what grounds, would shape later disagreements within Islam.
moments.note: These dates illuminate origins, not a fully formed pair of denominations. Sunni and Shi'a traditions developed over centuries, including differences in religious authority and practice. This short experience leaves much of that later history for further reading.

moments.title: Authority in dispute
moments.label: Political struggle
moments.body: Ali died in 661, and Umayyad rule took shape under Mu'awiya. Disagreement over leadership developed through political struggles within the Muslim community. These events were part of a longer history; Sunni and Shi'a traditions did not emerge fully formed in a single moment.
moments.note: The courtyard stays the same because this is a history within a shared Muslim community. The changing light is a metaphor for time, not a reconstruction of an event. The textbook's sections 8.8 and 8.9 provide a fuller account of the political struggles.

moments.title: A memory that endures
moments.label: Remembrance
moments.body: Husayn, Muhammad's grandson and Ali's son, was killed at Karbala in 680. His death became central to Shi'a remembrance of injustice and rightful leadership. Here, changes in light mark a moment for reflection; this imagined courtyard does not recreate Karbala or its violence.
moments.note: Karbala became central to Shi'a memory and commemoration. These three dates are a starting point, not a complete account of Sunni and Shi'a belief or practice. The source below offers further context, including later developments in the history of Islam.
